newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler, GM report April sales declines.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler, GM report April sales declines.

text.p: General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp., feeling the pain of labor strikes, reported lower U.S. April vehicle sales Thursday, while Toyota Motor Corp. posted its best April sales ever.
GM, the largest U.S. automaker, reported an April sales decline of 5.2 percent as total car and truck sales fell to 418,173 from 441,254 a year ago.

Chrysler finished April with total sales of 204,080, down from last year's April record of 230,469. Light truck sales were 134,166, down 9.8 percent, a bigger drop than analysts expected. Car sales tumbled almost 14 percent to 69,914.

"There's intense competition for car buyers as the market softens, with the industry shift toward the light truck segment," said James Holden, Chrysler's executive vice president of sales and marketing. "The softening is affecting all the major manufacturers, and Chrysler is no exception."
However, Toyota, the largest Japanese automaker, continued its strong showing this year with total April sales of 98,071, a 9.7 percent increase and a record for April.

Toyota's total car sales, riding the strength of record Camry demand, jumped 12.3 percent to 68,390. Total sport utility vehicle sales were up 7.8 percent to 16,675. Pickup truck sales rose 1.8 percent to 12,505.
"The outlook for the future is bright, and more sales records will fall," said Yale Gieszl, executive vice president of Toyota Motor Sales U.S.A.
Honda Motor Corp. also had an up month, with total sales rising 3 percent to 77,204. Highlights included the Civic small car, which had its best April ever with 26,894, a 2.3 percent increase.
GM's car sales were 236,562, a 12.6 percent decline from last year. Total truck sales rose 6.5 percent to 181,611 from 170,502. GM blamed its car sales decline on several factors.

The month-old strike at GM's Oklahoma City car plant deprived the company of an estimated 5,000 of the new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass mid-size sedans in April, said GM spokesman Dean Rotondo.

"The unfortunate thing is there was a great deal of momentum that was starting to generate surrounding the product," said Rotondo, who added GM has suspended all Malibu advertising until the strike is resolved.

Car sales also had a tough comparison to last year, when GM pushed through a large number of fleet sales. As it has for the last several months, GM said the phase-out of older models and the introduction of new models at initially lower volumes are holding sales back.

Rotondo said GM has been forced to resort to incentives to move its older model vehicles. April incentives continued at the relatively high level of $860 a vehicle GM had in North America for the first quarter, he said.

On the plus side, GM said the new Buick Century had its best April sales in six years, followed by the best Buick Park Avenue April sales in eight years. Total sales of the new minivans shot up 40 percent.

Truck sales, which rose more than analysts expected, were nevertheless held back by a two-week strike at GM's Pontiac, Mich., full-size pickup truck plant, which makes the most popular extended cab models.

Chrysler's Holden also said a three-week-old strike at the No. 3 U.S. automaker's Mound Road Engine plant in Detroit has caused "short-term uncertainty." The strike has cut off engines to most of Chrysler's truck plants in North America.

The few bright spots at Chrysler included the Sebring convertible, which had a monthly sales record of 6,182, a 24 percent increase. The Jeep Wrangler sport utility set an April record, with a 6 percent increase to 8,216.
The Ram full-size pickup truck, usually a hot-seller, fell 21 percent to 30,723. Chrysler's minivans as a group declined 11 percent to 45,191.

Other automakers that reported Thursday include: Mazda Motor Corp., which had a 10.7 percent drop in sales to 19,934; Mitsubishi Motor Corp., which had sales of 15,390, a rise of 1.6 percent; Subaru of America Inc., a unit of Fuji Heavy Industries Ltd., which had sales of 9,590, up 4.1 percent.
